newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam rules out joining coffee cartel soon.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam rules out joining coffee cartel soon.

text.p: Vietnam quashed growing hopes on Tuesday that it may join a global coffee producers' group, saying it was too poor to take part in a coordinated push to restrict exports and lift sagging prices.

Doan Trieu Nhan, Chairman of the Vietnam Coffee and Cocoa Association, said Hanoi had considered joining the 14-member Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC). But he said Vietnam lacked the administrative or financial capability to join now.
"Vietnam does not yet have a government coffee authority in charge of production as in other countries," he told Reuters. "We're also not financially capable of joining the ACPC retention plan."
An ACPC meeting on Thursday in Rio de Janeiro will consider a call by African producers to slice exports in the first half of this year by 2.5 million 60-kg (132-pound) bags to shore up prices.
However, Indonesia has expressed reservations about the plan and demanded that the Africans convince Vietnam to join the ACPC.

Traders said Vietnam, one of the poorest countries in the world, did not have the facilities to stock coffee to keep it off the market and its state-owned trading companies lacked sufficient access to credit to buy and hold stock on demand.
Nhan's comments should come as a particular disappointment to African producers, who are reeling from a slide in prices caused by an oversupply of arabica beans.
Ivory Coast Minister for Commodities Guy-Alain Gauze said on Tuesday Vietnam had expressed support for the ACPC and would consider joining.
Gauze's comments sent coffee futures soaring in London.
But a senior industry source in Vietnam said that while Hanoi had indeed indicated its support for the association, it would not be ready to join for several years.
Traders in Vietnam said the market should dismiss any hopes that Hanoi was even close to joining the ACPC.
"The Africans are absolutely scared and they are frightened that this is a highly efficient volume producer of robusta and they are going to be simply priced out of the market," one said.

"So they're screaming for Vietnam to join the ACPC and Vietnam is saying 'We don't need to. We're efficient. We're cheap. We can just produce volume and we don't need anything artificial to boost prices. We can still make money at these prices'."
Asia's largest coffee producer after Indonesia and the world's sixth-biggest exporter, Vietnam carries increasing weight in the world market.

Vietnam is expected to produce 270,000-280,000 tonnes of beans in the current 1996/97 crop -- a rise of about 17 percent from the year before -- and sell some 250,000 tonnes of that record crop abroad.

Desperate for the hard currency that coffee exports bring, the government is planning to grind out even more. It has set a plantation target for 2005 of at least 320,000 hectares (790,700 acres) compared with 200,000 (494,000 acres) now.
